title: A campus at eye level
caption: Six randomly drawn panoramas. Full 360° views with padding removed and the vegetation shares used in the analysis; all 13 are in Figure S1.
alt: Six labeled Street View panoramas of MIT, New York University, Barnard College, Macalester College, Pitzer College, and Claremont McKenna College with vegetation shares.
credit: Imagery © Google

title: Seeing one bus shelter three times
caption: Overlap correction at the University of Rochester, July 2015. (a) Version A keeps every panorama in the window and Version B one per 20 m unit; three sightings of one bus shelter, from panoramas 12–20 m away, merge where their bearing rays intersect. (b) The three detections; the match was checked visually, not by an independent labeler.
alt: Camera positions and bearing rays converge on one bus shelter, beside three labeled Rochester Street View images showing the same shelter.
credit: Imagery © Google

title: What computer vision counts
caption: Person and vehicle detections. YOLO with COCO classes at confidence ≥ 0.50, on four randomly drawn panoramas from four strata: at least four persons; at least eight vehicles; one to three vehicles and at least one person; and no detection at confidence 0.25.
alt: Four campus panoramas with colored bounding boxes for detected people and vehicles, and a labeled object legend.
credit: Street View imagery © Google; detections reproduced from the paper

title: Different streets, different campus conditions
caption: Within-campus variation at three campuses. Version B panoramas in the primary window, colored by green view, padding-corrected road share, and vehicles per panorama (color scales clipped at each campus’s 5th and 95th percentiles).
alt: A three-by-three map grid compares street greenery, corrected road share, and vehicle counts at the University of Chicago, Stanford University, and Colgate University.

title: Where parties make themselves visible
caption: Listed organizations of the six largest party lineages. Points mark coordinates classified as party organizations. White lines show provincial boundaries.
alt: Six maps of Turkey show the locations of listed AKP, CHP, MHP, İYİ, Saadet, and HDP/DEM party organizations.
qualityNote: Original PDF vectors exported as SVG with font outlines and the existing figure crop; axes, labels and legends preserved. Embedded raster panels retain their genuine source resolution; only vector content scales without a pixel limit.

title: Political symbols in the street
caption: Party symbols in election-period Street View imagery, with the annotators’ labels. Each panel shows a panorama tile from near a listed party office and gives the district, province, and capture month. The last panel shows overlapping displays from several parties.
alt: Eight labeled Street View panels show campaign flags and banners of Turkish parties, with human annotation boxes identifying the visible symbols.
credit: Street View imagery © Google; annotations reproduced from the paper

title: Whose symbols surround whose office?
caption: Whose symbols surround whose office. Each row groups labeled panoramas within 50 meters of an office of the named party, with a separate row for panoramas whose nearest listed site is a public institution. Each cell gives the percentage of panoramas in that row showing at least one symbol of the party named in the column.
alt: A yellow-to-red heatmap compares the share of panoramas showing each party’s symbols near that party’s and other parties’ offices.

title: Scholars across space and time
caption: Scholars in space and time
note: (a) Main place of activity. (b) Lifespans; (F) marks the three women and the faded segment the living scholar.
alt: A world map and lifespan timeline locate 23 religious and intellectual figures across Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Buddhism, and Hinduism.
qualityNote: Original PDF vectors exported as SVG with font outlines and the existing figure crop; axes, labels and legends preserved.

title: One scholar, different model portrayals
caption: Personas on the cultural map
note: Secular and emancipative values (Welzel 2013). Lines join each scholar’s BASE (open) and RAG (filled) positions. Grey points are WVS Wave 7 countries, with reference states labelled; dotted lines mark the least and most secular country.
alt: Six scatterplots place religious-scholar personas on secular and emancipative value axes, comparing six language models and retrieval conditions against World Values Survey country positions.
qualityNote: Original PDF vectors exported as SVG with font outlines and the existing figure crop; axes, labels and legends preserved.

title: Who takes the floor?
caption: Questioning in one Grand Chamber hearing. N.D. and N.T. v. Spain, 26 September 2018. The top strip identifies which side held the floor. Each row below represents a sitting judge, in order of precedence. Each mark represents a question unit, with color indicating the addressee.
alt: A hearing timeline shows the parties holding the floor and individual question marks for each of seventeen Grand Chamber judges in N.D. and N.T. v. Spain.
qualityNote: Original PDF vectors exported as SVG with font outlines and the existing figure crop; axes, labels and legends preserved.

title: The role of a seat on the bench
caption: Questioning by position on the bench. The figure shows the share of sittings in which a judge asked at least one question, with 95 percent intervals. Panel A groups sittings by role and defines senior positions as the first six ranks in the order of precedence. Panel B reports the share for each rank.
alt: Two interval plots compare questioning rates by bench role and by rank, showing a high questioning rate for national judges.
qualityNote: Original PDF vectors exported as SVG with font outlines and the existing figure crop; axes, labels and legends preserved.

title: Seventeen seats, unequal participation
caption: Seating and questioning rates. The figure shows the seats of the seventeen titular judges, numbered in order of precedence, with the presiding judge at the center. Each seat is labeled with the share of sittings in which its occupant asked a question.
alt: A semicircle of seventeen numbered judicial seats displays the percentage of sittings with a question for each seat.
qualityNote: Original PDF vectors exported as SVG with font outlines and the existing figure crop; axes, labels and legends preserved.

title: Real streets and generated cityscapes
caption: Comparison of (i) real Google Street View frames, (ii) SORA-generated frames, and (iii) Kling-generated frames for seven neighborhoods in Europe: (1) Christianshavn (Copenhagen, Denmark), (2) Laugardalur (Reykjavik, Iceland), (3) Temple Bar (Dublin, Ireland), (4) Ville Haute (Luxembourg City, Luxembourg), (5) De Pijp (Amsterdam, Netherlands), (6) Aker Brygge & Tjuvholmen (Oslo, Norway), and (7) Altstadt (Zurich, Switzerland).
alt: Seven rows compare real Google Street View images in the left column with Sora-generated images in the middle and Kling-generated images on the right.
credit: Real imagery: Google Street View. Synthetic frames: Sora and Kling, generated for the original study.
note: Columns two and three are synthetic research outputs, not photographs of the named places.

title: Campaign symbols around everyday places
caption: Disribution of Symbols Around Top Four Amenity Locations
alt: Four street maps show political symbols and concentric distance buffers around selected amenities in Ataşehir, Istanbul.
credit: Maps and symbol overlays reproduced from the author’s paper. Amenity data: OpenStreetMap.
note: All four locations are in the official district of Ataşehir, which has the greatest density of political symbols in the dataset.

title: Do models simulate similar responses?
caption: Correlation Table for LLM Output
alt: Two red correlation heatmaps compare sentiment outputs from ten language models before and after earthquake-related event scenarios.
note: The values are generated responses from hypothetical personas; they are not survey responses from earthquake survivors.

title: A citywide map of political visibility
caption: Symbol detection results from Istanbul
alt: Three Istanbul maps display Street View panorama coverage, political party symbols, and Atatürk and Turkish flag detections.

title: How the paper checks its fear scores
caption: These source-paper image pairs were shown to human annotators. In each original pair, the left image received a higher fear classification and the right image was a comparison; pair order was randomized for annotators. A model label should not be interpreted as proof of the person’s internal emotion.
alt: Six pairs of cable-news frames used in the paper’s human comparison of estimated fear expressions.
credit: Broadcast images from Fox News, CNN and MSNBC; reproduced from Ash and Caliskan’s research manuscript.

title: Comparing seven estimated expressions
caption: The original coefficient plots compare emotion classifications around opposing-party mentions. The joint and separate specifications both identify fear as the clearest positive relationship. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals; models account for the cable channel and detected word.
alt: Two original coefficient plots compare anger, disgust, happiness, fear, neutrality, sadness and surprise, with fear showing a positive association with opposing-party mentions.

title: Persistence, party and public topics
caption: The original parameter plot compares estimates for seven countries. Persistence in prior ties and same-party membership generally matter more than demographic similarity. The plotted intervals show the uncertainty reported in the manuscript; the networks represent shared hashtag use rather than direct conversations.
alt: An original interval plot compares intercept, age difference, prior-edge persistence, same-party and same-gender parameters across seven countries.

title: When ideological blocs move together or apart
caption: Six original panels compare the model’s within- and between-bloc attraction parameters. Positive values indicate modeled coalescence and negative values fragmentation over time, conditional on the network model. These estimates describe public discourse dynamics, not private bargaining or personal feelings.
alt: Six interval plots compare left–left, center–left, center–center, right–left, right–center and right–right attraction estimates across seven countries.

title: Street images and the depth model’s estimates
caption: Four source-paper examples pair images labeled Haifa, Jerusalem, Nazareth and Tel Aviv with outputs from the DepthAnything outdoor base model. The color fields are model-estimated depth, not ground-truth measurements.
alt: Four rows from the original paper compare urban street images with their colored predicted depth maps.
credit: Images and model outputs reproduced from the public research manuscript.

title: Comparing relative spacing across classified pairs
caption: The original YOLOv9e gender-merged specification plots normalized-distance estimates with 95% intervals. RA denotes the paper’s Religious Arab category, RJ Religious Jew, N Neutral, and NR Non-Religious. The red point shows the reference intercept; the other points show contrasts with that reference. Units are normalized, not meters.
alt: An original interval plot compares normalized-distance contrasts for ten pair categories, with same-group RA–RA and RJ–RJ contrasts below zero.

title: Estimating depth from a flat street image
caption: Final published article, Figure 3. The source’s depth-output example illustrates the attempt to distinguish foreground and background before estimating pairwise spacing. The color values are model output, not calibrated physical distance or a measure of a person’s identity. The complete source figure is reproduced without altering its contents.
alt: Original false-color depth map of a street scene, with people in the foreground and background.
credit: Caliskan et al., Scientific Reports (2025), Figure 3; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

title: Relative spacing across visible category pairs
caption: Final published article, Figure 5. Estimated contrasts in normalized distance from the cross-group reference, with the full specification’s controls. NRF/NRM mean non-religious female/male; RF/RM mean religious female/male as visually classified. Negative values indicate smaller relative distances, not fewer meters or proven political hostility. The complete source figure is reproduced without altering its contents.
alt: Coefficient plot showing especially negative normalized-distance estimates for pairs classified as religious women.
credit: Caliskan et al., Scientific Reports (2025), Figure 5; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

title: Agreement in ranking, compression in scale
caption: July 2024 SSRN/USC manuscript, Figure 3. The horizontal axis is the human-coded RILE benchmark and the vertical axis the model-derived score. The dashed identity line represents perfect agreement; flatter fitted model lines show compressed ideological differences. The original figure calls the benchmark “ground truth,” though the text discusses ambiguities in human coding.
alt: Scatterplot of five models’ RILE estimates against human manifesto scores, with fitted lines flatter than the identity line.
credit: Caliskan et al., Using Generative AI to Calculate Party Positions, July 2024 manuscript, Figure 3.

title: False claims combine several themes
caption: Final published article, Figure 3 (printed page 199). Diagonal cells count claims in each topic; other cells count topics appearing together. Colors use a logarithmic scale and blank cells indicate zero co-occurrences. These are coded items in a fact-check corpus, not population exposure or belief.
alt: Heatmap of COVID-19 falsehood topics and their co-occurrences, with counts printed in each cell.
credit: Caliskan and Kilicaslan, Journal of Computational Social Science, Figure 3; published online 2022.

title: Comparing content across press-freedom groups
caption: Final published article, Figure 13 (printed page 215), rotated for reading. Each row compares misinformation-content similarity within or between press-freedom categories. The within-group comparison for countries with a “very serious situation” has higher similarity and substantial variation. This is an association in selected fact-check records, not a causal estimate of censorship.
alt: Horizontal boxplots comparing misinformation similarity across pairs of press-freedom categories.
credit: Caliskan and Kilicaslan, Journal of Computational Social Science, Figure 13; published online 2022.

title: Daily changes in pandemic-related attention
caption: Final published article, Figure 8 (printed page 36). Stacked daily values show the paper’s computational topic-awareness measure for January–April 2020. Vertical lines mark first cases and policy dates. The figure shows changes in conversation and event timing; it does not measure the causal effect of a policy.
alt: Daily stacked bars of Ohio Twitter topic-awareness estimates, showing a large March increase in illness-related attention.
credit: Cantay Caliskan, Journal of Computational Social Science, Figure 8; published online 2021.

sourceFile: Final Wiley published article (HTML figure asset)
title: The policy network extends beyond ministers
caption: Final published article, Figure 1: Iceland Minister-to-Friend Network. Red nodes are ministers and gray nodes are accounts they follow. Shared gray nodes connect different ministers’ circles; a follow is a proxy for a relationship, not direct evidence of policy influence.
alt: Iceland’s minister-to-friend network, with red minister nodes and gray followed accounts in connected clusters.
credit: Caliskan (2020), Politics & Policy, Wiley.

sourceFile: Final Wiley published article (HTML figure asset)
title: Community structure and renewable-energy outcomes
caption: Final published article, Figure 8. Panels (a) and (b) show model-based marginal relationships for the last-ten-year and last-five-year outcome averages. Higher cross-community linkage and lower modularity are associated with higher renewable-energy outcomes; shaded uncertainty bands are part of the source figure. These are observational country comparisons, not causal effects.
alt: Six original marginal-effect plots, comparing cross-community links, modularity and centrality skewness with renewable-energy outcomes.
credit: Caliskan (2020), Politics & Policy, Wiley.

title: Research material: reference photo and AI-generated outputs
caption: Source Figure 1 uses prompts based on Kristi Noem’s characteristics. The left column repeats a real reference photograph. All fifteen images to its right are AI-generated research stimuli, arranged by generator and the attribute omitted from the prompt. They are not authentic portraits of Noem. Names were excluded from the generation prompts; the gallery is an example, not an estimate of an average effect.
alt: Source-paper comparison with a real reference photograph on the left and clearly identified AI-generated research outputs across three models and five masking conditions.
credit: Caliskan et al., The Imagined Congress, public SSRN manuscript, Figure 1.

title: Full information does not ensure a faithful distribution
caption: Source Figure 8 compares verified sample characteristics with the facial-analysis pipeline’s estimates for full-information (“Benchmark”) and masked-prompt (“Treatment”) portraits. The age distributions show a large youth shift even in the benchmark. Gender and race panels use the paper’s simplified binary categories; they summarize model classifications rather than identities.
alt: Original three-panel comparison of generated and verified age distributions, gender-category shares and race-category shares.
credit: Caliskan et al., The Imagined Congress, public SSRN manuscript, Figure 8.

title: Masking effects vary by platform and condition
caption: Source Figure 13 analyzes legislators recorded as women. The bottom panel compares masked prompts with the same politicians’ full-information prompts; negative treatment coefficients mean fewer woman-coded outputs. The Stable Diffusion differential is a comparison with the other platforms, not its complete effect. Its direction varies by condition, so the plot does not establish a universal benefit or harm from curation.
alt: Three coefficient panels with 95 percent confidence intervals for gender-classification changes among women legislators under different masking conditions and platform comparisons.
credit: Caliskan et al., The Imagined Congress, public SSRN manuscript, Figure 13.

title: Which part of the bird does each model select?
caption: Four multimodal-model rows compare the original image, predicted box mask, SAM-refined mask, and overlay. These are individual examples; the paper reports aggregate performance separately.
alt: Four model rows compare boxes and object masks for a bird in flight.
credit: Original figure from Caliskan and Chen, LUMOS.

title: The same lamp, different localizations
caption: A lamp example shows how different model localizations feed into the mask-refinement stage. A segmentation model can refine a useful box but cannot reliably repair a box placed over the wrong region.
alt: Four model rows compare masks and overlays for a red lamp on a table.
credit: Original figure from Caliskan and Chen, LUMOS.

title: Unusual observations as research leads
caption: Candidate outliers identified by the top methods are projected with CBLOF and robust scaling. Examples include post-conflict GDP changes and unusual combinations of health spending and health outcomes. The flagged cases invite substantive checking.
alt: Three panels show candidate country-year outliers with accompanying country labels.
credit: Original figure from Caliskan, Lelko, Noe, and Ogawa, ACROSS.

title: How many known outliers were recovered?
caption: The ensemble recovers about 54% of the labelled outlier observations on average, compared with about 15% for the Cook’s distance baseline. The benchmark contains 14 tasks with incomplete outlier labels; recall and F1 should be read in that context.
alt: Original comparison table with mean recall near 0.54 for ACROSS and 0.15 for Cook’s distance.
credit: Original table from Caliskan, Lelko, Noe, and Ogawa, ACROSS.

title: What the vegetation detector keeps
caption: Five panorama pairs show the original street-level image on the left and DEVISE output on the right, with detected vegetation emphasized in green. The examples illustrate measurement behavior rather than a quantitative accuracy benchmark.
alt: Five paired street panoramas compare the original view with highlighted detected vegetation.
credit: Original figure from the DEVISE manuscript. Street imagery © Google.

title: Three counties, two ways to count greenery
caption: The top row maps the sampled Street View locations in Bucks, Dauphin, and Washington counties. The next rows compare plain pixel-count greenness with depth-aware estimates; colors are normalized across the panorama corpus.
alt: Nine maps show sampled locations, baseline greenery, and depth-aware greenery for three U.S. counties.
credit: Original figure from the DEVISE manuscript.

title: Mapping generated profiles beside survey responses
caption: Rows use mean, median, and modal response summaries; columns use PCA, UMAP, and t-SNE. Larger squares represent generated scholar profiles and smaller circles represent contemporary country aggregates. The projections are exploratory, not validation of a historical thinker’s beliefs.
alt: Nine scatterplots compare generated scholar profiles and contemporary country aggregates under three projection methods.
credit: Original figure from Caliskan and colleagues, HalalLLM vs. KosherLLM.

title: The response pattern behind an average
caption: Median responses are displayed by survey item and scholar–model combination. Color shows the coded response value; white marks responses outside the acceptable range. Different items use different scales, so color alone is not a common ideological score.
alt: Dense heatmap of median coded World Values Survey responses across scholar and model combinations.
credit: Original figure from Caliskan and colleagues, HalalLLM vs. KosherLLM.

title: The LEGO-style propaganda corpus
caption: Selected stills from fifteen distinct animations in the corpus, by provenance (rows) and upload date (left to right). Titles are shortened from the upload title or on-screen title; channel is the uploading account. Regime-linked videos are mostly re-uploads of animations credited to Explosive Media (Akhbar-e Enfejari) or other Iranian producers.
alt: Fifteen labeled stills from AI-generated LEGO-style propaganda videos, organized into regime-linked producers, Iran-aligned accounts, and trend adopters. These are study materials, not photographs of real events.
note: AI-generated LEGO-style propaganda reproduced and analyzed in the paper. These synthetic scenes are research material; they do not document real events. Provenance categories do not establish direct state control.

title: Selective suffering, fantasy, and circulation
caption: Tests of the H2 hypotheses. (a) Coefficient on an Iranian perpetrator in regressions of victim suffering among violent scenes with an identified perpetrator; the top rows use the standardized suffering index, the component rows its six elements on their own scales. (b) Within-video coefficients on scene type in regressions of fantasticality with video fixed effects. (c) Coefficients on standardized humor and alternative measures in circulation models; outcomes and estimators are identified by row. All intervals are 95 percent; standard errors clustered by video for fixed-effects models and by channel otherwise.
alt: Three original interval plots show lower depicted suffering for Iranian-perpetrated violence, small fantasticality differences by scene type, and no reliable within-channel humor–view association.
note: Outcomes measure representations in animated videos and collection-time engagement, not real-world suffering or causal persuasion.

title: Historical architecture, in game and in reference images
caption: Examples of image-based comparison of game architecture and real-world reference structures
alt: Labeled pairs compare in-game and reference depictions of the Dome of the Rock, Tikal, Salisbury Cathedral, Notre-Dame, the Statue of Zeus, Epidaurus, Stonehenge, Westminster Abbey, Palais Garnier, and Château de Chantilly.
note: Original game screenshots and reference images reproduced in the research paper. Architectural resemblance is only one dimension of historical representation.

title: Matching a building’s details across a photograph and a game
caption: LightGlue local feature matching approach.
alt: The paper’s LightGlue example links green architectural keypoints and orange correspondence lines between a real-world building photograph and its in-game representation.
note: Local feature correspondence illustrates a different measurement target from broad image resemblance; viewpoint and reference selection also affect the score.

title: From a courtroom frame to classifier probabilities
caption: The pipeline applied to one frame (2016 hearing). Note: In (d), the anger share is this face’s usual reading. Frame © ECHR-CEDH.
alt: An original four-panel figure shows an ECHR hearing frame, face detections, tracked identities, and expression-classifier probabilities over time. The probability labels describe model outputs, not judges’ feelings.
credit: Frame © ECHR-CEDH.
note: Facial-expression classifier outputs cannot establish a judge’s internal emotional state. Printed page19; PDF page20.

title: When head orientation changes an apparent party difference
caption: Head orientation and the difference between parties (exploratory). Note: (a, b) Same judges, one 2015 hearing. (c) Listening seconds. (d) Within judge-hearing, seconds with neither party speaking; bands = 95% CI. (e) Estimates with 95% CIs. Frames © ECHR-CEDH.
alt: Original ECHR frames compare judges facing each party. Histograms, response curves, and interval plots show that accounting for head orientation removes most of the apparent negative-display difference between government and applicant turns.
credit: Frames © ECHR-CEDH.
note: The orientation analyses are exploratory. These are classifier probabilities rather than direct measures of emotion. Printed page32; PDF page33.
